text: Final Technical Report 47/57 Changes in Benthic and Pelagic Habitat The presence of the MTV and, in some cases, independently moored CECs will require anchors in the seabed and mooring cables through the water column or jack-up feet and columns. Installations like this have the potential to alter habitats, affecting the animals that rely on them, particularly benthic habitats [15]. The MTV, CECs, and site selected could impact this consideration. Results of deployments from other offshore industries and research studies can inform likely outcomes of the placement and operation of the MTV and test CECs on benthic and pelagic habitats. The MTV and moored CECs must be sited away from rare or fragile habitats. Entanglement in Mooring Lines There are concerns that large marine animals could become entangled or trapped in mooring lines and power export cables, often marine mammals (site dependent). This concern stems from entanglement, injury, and death of marine mammals and sea turtles from lost and abandoned fishing gear. This risk is not analogous to marine energy or the proposed MTV mooring system(s), as there are no loose ends of lines or slack lines creating loops that might entangle animals [16]. Haul Out or Roosting of Seabirds Concerns have been raised by stakeholders and regulators that seals and sea lions might haul out, and seabirds might roost on floating hulls. Although there is little likelihood of harm to the animals from this behavior, the design of the hull can be made to discourage or make this behavior not possible, including creating a lack of level space for pinnipeds to haul out and a rough or spiky surface that will discourage bird roosting. This concern is MTV design, CEC configuration (if it is a floating turbine concept), and site dependence, and it can be addressed with inexpensive and simple design modifications. Displacement of Animals from Critical Habitats The presence of many floating structures or turbines might create a barrier effect or displace marine animals from the critical habitats they need for success. This effect could occur from the presence of the CEC, seabed anchors, or water column mooring lines. Little research or insight has been gathered about this potential interaction, as the current thinking is that small numbers of CECs (one to perhaps four) are unlikely to cause this effect [17]. Because the MTV will not present a significant barrier effect by itself and is designed to support single CEC testing, it is not likely to significantly displace animals from critical habitats. 13.4.2 Impact of Regulatory Considerations The MTV is an unpowered barge expected to be located in specific locations for short durations and would be subject to conventional barge considerations. The MTV is expected to pose a minimal regulatory risk based on the identified regulatory considerations. Rather, the greatest expected regulatory impact on authorizing MTV use is from individual CEC configurations and sites selected for testing.
